summary: Marin sits just north of the Golden Gate Bridge yet manages to keep nearly 80% of its 526 square miles as open space, parkland, or agricultural preserve — a ratio almost unheard of for a county bordering a major metro. The western half is dominated by Point Reyes National Seashore and the rolling grasslands of the Marin Agricultural Land Trust, while the eastern corridor along Highway 101 holds the bulk of the population in a string of small towns — San Rafael, Mill Valley, Tiburon, Novato — tucked into redwood canyons and along bay shorelines. Mount Tamalpais anchors the landscape at roughly 2,570 feet, offering trail networks that drop from fog-line ridges to tidal marshes within a single afternoon hike. The tradeoff for all that beauty is stark: a median home price near $1.39 million against a median household income of about $143,000 yields a price-to-income ratio around 9.7, meaning even the local median earner faces a significant gap to ownership. Much of the employment base is in healthcare, education, and professional services, but the county functions substantially as a bedroom community for San Francisco, with Golden Gate Transit and ferry service from Larkspur carrying commuters across the bay. Daily highs average a mild 66°F with nearly nine hours of sunshine, though summer fog regularly pours through gaps in the coastal hills and can hold morning temperatures in the low 50s well into July. Marin is a place where the physical environment is genuinely extraordinary and the economics of participating in it are genuinely punishing — that tension defines nearly every housing decision made here.
